Chapter 10. The Children—Growing Up in the Shadow of Instability.
When kids go through eviction, it's a kind of heartbreak that sticks with them. Think about it—the place they called home, the routines they relied on, even the friendships they built—suddenly, all of that disappears. That sense of safety and belonging just evaporates.
Imagine a boy who's always been outgoing and full of life. After his family loses their home, he retreats into himself. School becomes a struggle. His grades slip, and he can’t quite find his footing in a new classroom. Old friends are left behind, but moving so often makes it tough to build new connections. At night, he hears his mother crying softly, and the uncertainty weighs on him in ways he can’t quite name.
Teachers start to pick up on the signals—he’s got tired eyes, sometimes homework goes missing, and there are sudden absences. They want to help, but the resources just aren’t there. And with all the moves, learning gets interrupted again and again. It’s hard for him to keep pace with his lessons, or even join in with activities. That bright confidence he once had? It starts to crumble, replaced by anxiety and self-doubt.
The truth is, instability like this leaves a mark that lasts long after the boxes are unpacked. Kids who go through eviction are more likely to have a tough time in school, drop out altogether, or wrestle with mental health problems. Losing a home doesn’t just shake their world—it shapes how they see themselves, making it hard to trust or feel safe.
Most of us never see how deeply eviction affects children. It’s easy to focus on the crisis as it happens, but those effects don’t fade away—they linger, sometimes for years. One lost home can set off a chain reaction that makes it so much harder to recover.
So, here’s the key takeaway: the real cost of eviction isn’t just counted in lost houses. It’s measured in lost potential, in dreams that get put on hold or broken before they even begin.
